description: We are a team of enthusiastic young innovators from Apeejay School, Haldia, comprising students of Classes VIII and IX. Passionate about astronomy, space technology, coding, and scientific exploration, we are developing an interactive website to simulate lunar landing sites for spacecraft. We believe in creativity, teamwork, and turning curiosity into innovation. Think Beyond Earth. Explore Beyond Limits!
summary:
AstraLune: Bridging the Ephemeris-to-Execution Gap at the Lunar South Pole

AstraLune is a browser-based mission-planning suite built for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, Lunar Landing Site Navigator. It turns raw lunar topographic and orbital data into an intuitive Flight-Director interface for evaluating landing sites at the lunar South Pole, where grazing sunlight, deep permanent shadows, and Earth's libration can make or break power, thermal, and communication margins. The platform combines four modules: a Three.js 3D renderer of terrain and orbital geometry, a skyplot and terrain heatmap with a surface traverse planner, a full launch-to-descent mission visualizer with live telemetry, and "Edith," a multimodal AI co-pilot paired with a hands-free gesture laboratory. Together they produce an immediate Go/No-Go feasibility assessment, letting engineers run rapid trade-off studies and letting students and the public grasp the engineering realities of polar exploration. AstraLune compresses work that once required disjointed scripts into a single visual workspace, flagging power starvation, slope hazards, and communication blackouts before any propellant is committed.
details:
AstraLune – Project Details

AstraLune is an interactive lunar mission-planning platform that we developed for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge – Lunar Landing Site Navigator. The idea behind this project is to make it easier to understand one of the biggest challenges of future lunar exploration: finding a safe and suitable place to land near the Moon’s South Pole.

While working on AstraLune, we wanted to bring different aspects of lunar exploration together in one place. This includes 3D lunar visualisation, scientific analysis, mission simulations, and AI assistance. Instead of simply looking at maps and scientific data, users can explore the lunar surface and understand the factors that influence landing-site selection.

1. What does the project do, and how does it work?

AstraLune works like a digital mission-control workspace where users can explore potential lunar landing sites and examine the conditions that could affect a mission.

Some of its main features are:

  • 3D Lunar Terrain Viewer: Allows users to explore an interactive 3D representation of the Moon and examine possible landing regions.
  • Landing-Site Analysis: Evaluates factors such as elevation, slope, surface roughness, and potential hazards. It also includes a hazard heatmap and a GO/NO-GO assessment for the selected landing area.
  • Illumination and Earth Visibility: Helps users understand how sunlight availability and visibility of Earth change depending on the selected planning time.
  • Mission Simulation: Provides a visual simulation of a journey from Earth to the Moon, including the lunar approach and descent, along with mission phases and telemetry information.
  • Scenario Comparison: Allows users to compare different landing locations based on illumination, Earth visibility, terrain conditions, power availability, and scientific value.
  • Edith AI Co-Pilot: Acts as an AI assistant that answers questions related to lunar missions and helps users understand the available mission information. It can also connect to the Gemini API for AI-generated responses.
  • Voice and Gesture Interaction: Supports voice commands, spoken responses, and hand gestures, making the platform more interactive.
  • Learning and Mission Challenges: Includes educational activities that help users understand the decisions and trade-offs involved in planning a lunar mission.

We also made sure to distinguish between actual sourced observations, calculated results, proxy data, and synthetic demonstration data. We believe this is important because users should know whether the information they are viewing comes from real scientific sources or is being used for demonstration purposes.

2. What benefits does it have?

AstraLune offers several benefits, especially for people interested in space science and lunar exploration.

  • Makes complex lunar mission concepts easier to understand through interactive 3D visualisation.
  • Helps users compare different landing locations instead of judging them based on just one factor.
  • Identifies potential terrain hazards and highlights possible landing difficulties.
  • Demonstrates how sunlight, communication, power availability, and surface conditions affect mission planning.
  • Provides students and space enthusiasts with an engaging way to learn about lunar exploration.
  • Encourages users to make informed decisions by showing the sources and reliability of the available data.

Our main focus was to make scientific information easier to explore without losing the technical aspects that make lunar mission planning challenging.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our aim with AstraLune is to make the challenges of future lunar exploration easier to understand and explore, particularly in the Moon's South Polar region.

Choosing a lunar landing site is not just about finding a flat area. Factors such as sunlight, communication with Earth, surface conditions, temperature, and scientific importance all play a role. We wanted to bring these factors together so users could understand how they are connected and why each one matters.

We hope AstraLune can be useful for students, educators, researchers, and anyone interested in space exploration. It could also serve as a starting point for developing more advanced lunar mission-planning tools in the future.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

We developed AstraLune mainly as a browser-based application, using web technologies and different interactive libraries.

Here are the main technologies we used and how they contributed to the project:

Technol ogy

How we used it

HTML5

Built the basic structure and layout of the platform.

CSS3

Designed the interface, animations, layouts, and responsive elements.

JavaScript

Handled the application logic, scientific calculations, simulations, and interactive features.

Three.js

Created the 3D lunar terrain, Earth–Moon visualisation, and orbital representations.

Tailwind CSS

Helped us build a responsive and consistent interface.

Font Awesome

Provided icons for different interface elements.

MediaPipe Hands

Enabled webcam-based hand tracking and gesture interaction.

Google Gemini API

Supported optional AI-generated responses through Edith.

Web Speech API

Enabled voice recognition and text-to-speech features.

Web Audio API

Was used for interface sounds and audio effects.

HTML Canvas

Helped us create hazard maps, charts, and other visual elements.

Browser Local Storage

Saved selected scenarios and user preferences.

Hardware requirements: AstraLune can run on a regular computer or laptop with a modern web browser. A webcam is needed for gesture-based interaction, while a microphone is useful for voice commands. No specialised hardware is required to use the main platform.

We also referred to NASA lunar data resources, including LOLA and LROC. The current version combines sourced references with calculated results, proxy terrain information, and synthetic demonstration values. We have included distinctions between these categories so that users can understand what is verified and what is estimated or simulated.

5. How is your project creative?

What makes AstraLune different is the way it brings several technologies together to create an interactive lunar mission-control experience.

We didn't want to build just another website with maps, charts, and blocks of scientific information. Instead, we wanted users to feel like they were working inside a lunar mission-control environment.

Users can explore the Moon in 3D, examine potential landing locations, compare different mission scenarios, and watch simulated mission phases. They can also interact with the platform using voice commands and hand gestures.

One of our most interesting features is Edith, the AI Co-Pilot. It allows users to ask mission-related questions in natural language rather than having to understand every technical term or search through different sections manually.

We also focused on the overall design. The interface takes inspiration from aerospace mission-control systems, featuring telemetry displays, mission-status indicators, hazard maps, scenario comparisons, and a dark visual theme.

By combining scientific exploration with AI assistance and interactive controls, we wanted to create something that is not only informative but also enjoyable to explore.

6. What factors did your team consider?

While developing AstraLune, we considered several scientific, technical, and practical factors that could influence a lunar landing mission.

  1. Terrain Safety: We considered surface elevation, slope, roughness, craters, and other possible landing hazards to understand whether an area could be suitable for landing.
  2. Solar Illumination: We looked at sunlight availability because solar energy can play an important role in powering lunar equipment and supporting mission operations.
  3. Communication: We considered visibility between the landing site and Earth, as maintaining communication is important for mission coordination.
  4. Power Availability: We explored how sunlight, energy requirements, and battery reserves could affect the operation of a lunar mission.
  5. Temperature Conditions: We considered the extreme temperature conditions around the lunar South Pole and their possible impact on equipment and mission operations.
  6. Scientific Value: We considered the scientific importance of different regions, including areas near permanently shadowed regions that could be valuable for future exploration.
  7. Landing Constraints: We included illustrative landing requirements to assess whether a selected region meets the simulator's landing criteria.
  8. Data Reliability: We made an effort to distinguish between verified observations, calculated values, proxy information, and synthetic data.
  9. User Accessibility: We wanted the platform to be easy to explore, so we included visual, voice-based, and gesture-based interaction.
  10. Future Development: We designed the platform with future improvements in mind, allowing additional datasets, better scientific models, and more advanced mission-planning features to be integrated later.

Conclusion

AstraLune was born from a vision to transform how we explore, analyse, and plan lunar landing missions.

By bringing together advanced 3D lunar visualisation, scientific terrain analysis, mission simulation, AI-powered assistance, and intuitive voice and gesture interactions, AstraLune creates an integrated environment for exploring the complexities of lunar exploration.

At its core, AstraLune is built around a powerful idea: every successful lunar mission begins with an informed decision. Selecting a landing site requires more than identifying a location. It demands a deeper understanding of lunar topography, surface conditions, environmental constraints, and mission requirements. AstraLune brings these interconnected elements together in one interactive platform.

But our vision extends beyond today's capabilities. We see AstraLune evolving into a more comprehensive lunar mission-planning ecosystem, with increasingly sophisticated scientific analysis, enhanced simulation capabilities, richer datasets, and intelligent decision-support systems.

Our ambition is not just to explore the Moon through technology, but to make the technologies behind lunar exploration more accessible to the next generation of innovators.

With AstraLune, we are taking a step towards a future where curiosity drives innovation, technology expands possibilities, and the next chapter of space exploration begins with bold ideas.
